=== page: current-state/index.html
title: Current State — The Future of Case Management IT
description: What 326 service-delivery procedures show about how the work is actually done.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT

Current State
The design is not a simple contradiction of the current system. It is the result of an interrogation as to why a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of intelligent, well-intended, capable people can fail to meet the needs of the organizations it is meant to serve. The conclusion is that the mismatch is not about what is present in the current system, but what is absent, ignored, or externalized.
What the SDPR procedures are
Every recurring task a caseworker performs has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as it is actually delivered.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it implements, the legislation behind it, and how the work is classified in the system. That makes the whole set readable as a map of the services.
326procedures
15capability areas
128kinds of work request
84statutory provisions cited
146distinct forms
13ways to reach the ministry
Work crosses system boundaries constantly
63% of documented procedures need two or more systems to finish one task.
Number of procedures by count of separate systems required, across 326 procedures.
Systems
Procedures
Proportion
0
39
1
80
2
114
3
51
4+
42
Highlighted rows are the 207 procedures that cross a system boundary. Four procedures require seven.
Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.
One journey, three systems, two re-keys
Recovering an overpayment is the clearest example. A worker who has decided that someone was paid too much must:
Open a separate web application to calculate the amount. It does not connect to either system of record.
Print the result, scan it, and attach it back to the case.
Move the case file to their own office in the mainframe so they have permission to act on it.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Move the case file back to where it came from.
For clients whose earnings are annualised there is a further step: a spreadsheet, with figures read off one screen, typed into the spreadsheet, and the result typed back.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. It is written down as the correct procedure, because given the systems that exist it is the correct procedure.
Where the rules actually live
A modernisation needs to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement are in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
Business rules by location
Where
What it holds
A rules engine
29 separate rulebases covering eligibility, validation, debt and payment calculation
The mainframe
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Formulas inside the case system
Retention periods, access levels, privacy calculations
A database table
The rates the public-facing eligibility estimator uses
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. No source control, promotion pipeline or version register is documented for the 29 rulebases.
Routing runs on a spreadsheet
Which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes are all defined in an Excel workbook that 56 procedures refer to. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. Priority and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, maintained by hand.
Accommodation and the signature problem
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have limited computer access: a worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
Because that path skips portal registration, no personal identification number is created for the applicant. The electronic signature depends on that number. The people the accommodation exists for are the people who cannot then sign electronically.
How these figures were produced
All counts and analysis were derived from a comprehensive examination of the Resource Finder and other document repositories. This corpus was analyzed, pattern-matched and mapped. Named systems, capability areas and procedure backing were derived from the documents and the policy manual.
Volumetrics are not yet calculated. Caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth can be measured, but in this analysis they were drawn from the technical design documents.
These design pages set out how the proposal resolves these conditions. The clearest place to see the connection is evidence, because the overpayment journey above is a direct consequence of a record that cannot say what was known and when.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document and from 326 service-delivery procedures. Nothing here is a government commitment.

=== page: decisions/index.html
title: Decisions — The Future of Case Management IT
description: The least conventional decisions in the design, what each is for, and what it costs.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Decisions
Decisions
Several decisions here are not what a team would reach for by default. Each is set out with what it buys and what it costs, so that a reader can disagree with it specifically.
01 Store dated claims, not facts –
Why it is unusual
Most case systems store the current value of a field and log changes separately.
What it is for
Whether a person owes money back depends on whether the ministry knew something and failed to act. A current value with a change log beside it cannot answer that reliably, because the log is not part of the decision path.
What it costs
Every read is more complex. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and reporting has to specify which point in time it means.
02 Track two kinds of time, and inherit a third +
Why it is unusual
Bitemporal modelling is well established in finance and rare in case management.
What it is for
The two questions a tribunal asks are what was true and what the ministry knew. They need separate axes. The third axis exists only because fifteen years of records arrive from a system that is still running, and collapsing their history into the migration date would make an entire class of question unanswerable.
What it costs
More storage, and a real learning curve. The third axis will be unknown in most inherited records, and the system has to say so rather than guess.
03 Five case models rather than one +
Why it is unusual
The conventional move is a single configurable case model shared across programs.
What it is for
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model makes every change a negotiation, and the previous programme cut scope rather than change one.
What it costs
Plumbing gets written five times. This is a real cost and it is accepted deliberately.
04 Decisions read no live data +
Why it is unusual
Rules engines are usually called as a service that fetches what it needs while it runs.
What it is for
If a decision reads anything not stored with it, it cannot be reproduced. Reproduction is the difference between showing a tribunal what happened and reconstructing it from memory.
What it costs
The facts have to be assembled before the decision runs, and assembling them consistently is its own problem.
05 The interface outlives its implementation +
Why it is unusual
Translation layers over a legacy system are normally treated as the durable asset.
What it is for
Replacing a system in pieces only works if consumers are insulated from which piece is answering. The published interface is permanent; the translation layer behind it is temporary and its team is accountable for disbanding.
What it costs
It requires refusing legacy vocabulary in the published interface even when exposing it would be faster.
06 Store the letter, not just the decision +
Why it is unusual
Correspondence is usually treated as output rather than part of the record.
What it is for
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what was computed. A determination that reproduces perfectly alongside an unreconstructable letter does not answer the question.
What it costs
Template versions and content hashes have to be retained for as long as the decisions that reference them.
07 Retention lives on the type, not the storage location +
Why it is unusual
Retention is commonly inferred from where something is stored.
What it is for
Inference from location fails the first time a fact appears in two places, which is the first day. Attaching classification and retention to the kind of evidence makes disposition tractable.
What it costs
Every evidence type needs a records determination before it can be used, which puts the records office on the critical path.
How the design was arrived at
The architecture document marks every claim with how well it is supported: verified against a primary source, internally confirmed but not publicly checkable, derived by arithmetic from marked inputs, or unverified. Unverified claims carry an owner and a date by which someone must resolve them.
That convention produced a section most architecture documents do not have: a list of things the authors believed at the outset and then disproved. Eleven assumptions were tested and failed. Two examples.
System residency is a legal requirement
Neither the federal nor the provincial statute book requires systems to be located in Canada for government applications, and no published policy stipulating it could be found.
The design still keeps systems in Canada, because cloud policy independently requires Canadian data centres. What changed is the stated reason, which is now policy rather than law.
Replacing the existing system has a deadline
Vendor support for the current platform is committed through at least December 2037, on a rolling ten-year basis.
Nothing external forces the replacement to finish. Anything that does has to be built into how the programme is run, which is why the design says so plainly rather than assuming urgency.
Two of eleven assumptions that did not survive testing. Recording them makes the design reviewable; an architecture whose failed premises are invisible cannot be checked.
What the evidence base is
Two bodies of source material sit behind this. The technical design documents for the current release of the existing system, 57 of them, describing the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting. And the 326 service-delivery procedures describing how the work is done.
Reading both matters, because they disagree about what the system is. The technical documents describe 61 applications. The procedures reveal 28 further tools that a worker actually touches and that appear in no technical document: a standalone calculator, a reporting tool, credit and asset-check portals, a worker-safety device, a vital statistics service.
What remains unresolved
The architecture carries 40 open verification items and 30 items that must be resolved before the design is frozen. Three are worth naming here because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
Whether the rules can be migrated independently of the mainframe, given that both calculate.
Whether the decision on what the third time axis holds can be made before the first production record is written. It cannot be added afterwards.
What service levels the analytical platform can commit to, which depends on a storage benchmark that has not yet been run.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

=== page: determinations/index.html
title: Determinations — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why an entitlement decision is treated as a function that can be re-run years later.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Decisions
Determinations
A decision about someone's entitlement may be challenged years after it was made. The design treats every decision as something that can be re-run rather than remembered.
The problem with asking a system what it decided
Ask a typical case management system why a person received a particular amount in March 2022 and it will recalculate. It will use today's rules, today's data and today's software, and report the answer with confidence. That answer may be right. There is no way to tell, and no way to show a tribunal the difference.
Three things have moved underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, possibly several times. The software itself was upgraded, and a rules engine upgrade can alter how the same rule evaluates without anyone noticing until someone appeals.
Treating a decision as a function
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. It does not read the clock, does not query a database, and does not call another service while it runs. Everything it needs is handed to it.
That constraint sounds academic. It is what makes the next part possible: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The function signature
Determine(rulesArtefactVersion, evidenceSnapshot, referenceDate) → DeterminationResult
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine provides this on its own; it is enforced by the shell around the engine. The engine evaluates in-process against a snapshot passed by value, which is what makes byte-identical replay achievable rather than aspirational.
Five things stored with every decision
Storing the answer is not enough, and storing the answer plus the rules is still not enough. Five artefacts are bound into the record at the moment the decision is made.
1 The rules Content digest, tagged and immutable once released Stored
2 The engine Version number and the archived binary Stored
3 The facts it saw Copied in full into the record, never referenced Stored
4 The reasoning Which rules fired and which branches were taken, in a ministry-owned format Stored
5 The letter Content-hashed template, resolved at decision time Stored
The decision can be replayed.
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.
Switch any artefact off to see which question stops being answerable. Each one covers a failure the other four do not.
The fifth is the one most often left out. A determination that reproduces perfectly, paired with a letter nobody can reconstruct, does not answer the question a tribunal actually put, which is frequently about what the person was told rather than what the system computed.
How long replay has to work
Archiving the software guarantees you can identify it. It does not guarantee that anything in twenty years can run it. The operating system, the processor architecture and the container runtime all have shorter lives than a child protection record, which is retained for ninety years.
Rather than leave that unresolved, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Years 0–7
The software itself is archived and tested quarterly to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that actually re-execute.
Years 7–20
The rules are maintained as a written specification, with a test suite that any re-implementation must reproduce. The suite is kept independent of the engine from the first day, so this transition costs nothing when it arrives.
Beyond 20 years
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record, and re-running is no longer offered. This is what a paper file has always been.
The three stages are a real sequence, which is why they are numbered. The last is defensible because it was declared in advance rather than discovered during a hearing.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently, and that is where the remaining gap sits.
Assembling the facts means reading across several stores that update independently. Two decisions issued seconds apart, where one store is briefly behind, can legitimately see different worlds. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far detects it. The design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events, so a later reader can tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Decisions that affect people carry their own classification
Every rule is labelled with what kind of decision it produces: an administrative decision that requires reasons, a decision that a person must make before it takes effect, or an intermediate calculation that affects nobody on its own.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. An adverse determination emits its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it because the classification says it must, not because somebody remembered.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

=== page: domains/index.html
title: Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the design uses sixteen separate models rather than one, and the rules that keep them separate.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Decisions
Domains
The most consequential choice in this design is where to draw lines between parts of the system, and then to defend those lines. Twelve domain models, one of which is really five, so sixteen in total.
The argument against a single model
Programmes like this usually begin by building one model of a case that every program can share. It looks like the responsible choice: less duplication, one place to change things, consistency across the ministry.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Making them share a lifecycle means every change to one is negotiated with everyone else. The model becomes something nobody can change, and the programme starts removing scope to avoid changing it. The previous programme here merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope, for exactly this reason.
So the design accepts duplication. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
What the parts are
Shared spine
Participant Identity
Evidence & Verification
Eligibility & Entitlement
One per program family
Employment assistance
Child protection
Child care subsidy
Employment services
Persons with disabilities
Money
Payments & Issuance
Financial Components
Overpayment & Recovery
Delivery
Appeals & Reconsideration
Work Management
Documents & Capture
Notices & Correspondence
Provider & Outcome
Evidence & Verification
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Owns
The evidence succession set, verification policy, the four operations, three time axes.
Does not own
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
Boundary test
Its events are the trigger fabric for everything else.
Select any part to see what it owns, what it deliberately does not own, and the test that tells you when the boundary has been breached. The five case models share protocols, not a case model.
Four rules keep the lines in place
A boundary that exists only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These are written so that a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
Each part can be released on its own
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always have to ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This is the rule that erodes first and takes the longest to notice.
There are exactly two ways to talk
A published interface for reads, and published events for notifications. There is no third mechanism, and adding one is not a shortcut.
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
A part needing another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events, shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
The thin identity model
Participant Identity is deliberately small: identifiers, enough detail to tell two people apart, and whether identity has been proven. Not addresses, not income, not relationships.
This is the part most likely to drift, because every new requirement produces a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model has been rebuilt in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Merge and split are built in from the first day rather than added later. The previous system's audit found duplicate records at scale, with search described as ineffective and exact-match only. Retrofitting merge into a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible, because by then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would be stable.
Published events and the boundary test
Participant Identity publishes PersonRegistered, IdentityMerged, IdentitySplit, IdentifierAdded and IdentifierInvalidated. Every other context maintains its own projection (Payee, Applicant, Caregiver, Reporter, Appellant, Debtor) keyed by participant identifier.
Evidence & Verification publishes EvidenceRecorded, EvidenceActivated, EvidenceSuperseded, EvidenceVerified, EvidenceInvalidated and EvidenceCorrectionRecorded.
Parts that are not domain models
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. They are owned by platform teams and used by everyone. The distinction matters because a platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a seventeenth domain model without anyone chartering it.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters are deliberately opposite. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive the systems that implement it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it is accountable for its own disbandment.
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

=== page: evidence/index.html
title: Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the system records dated claims rather than facts, and why it tracks two kinds of time.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Decisions
Evidence
ICM tracks facts. Fields are overwritten, history is obscured. In the new system, the unit of informationv is not a "fact" it is a timestamped, attributable claim linked to evidence. That claim can be falsified, validated, overturned or replaced - and no information is lost.
Why not store facts?
A system that stores just the current state, "Income: $900" has left unanswered some of the most important questions. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number or the number recorded at the time? Frontline staff are adaptable, this information isn't truly lost it's just not modeled by the system. It goes in notes, forms, attachments and other ancillary documents, only the tiny slice of information is actually held as data.
This isn't simply an auditing nicety, it eliminates the cognitive drag; the mismatch between how the system handles data and how frontline staff operate. Significant effort is spent substantiating evidence against claims, this is done manually and is not a properly modeled first class activity despite it being, numerically, the most common task workers perform. Social workers must spend hours mapping their notes and activities to a different structure - serving the software, rather than their clients.
So the unit of storage is an assertion:
what household composition: couple
about whomparticipant 4471-A
true forfrom 1 January, open-ended
learned on12 September
fromeligibility review finding
verifiedtenancy agreement, 14 September
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are contested. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It came to that view in September. Eight months of payments were made at the single rate in between, and which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.
The four things that can happen to an assertion
Once something is recorded it is never edited in place. Four operations change what the system believes, and they differ in one respect: what each does to the period the claim covers.
[aria-label] Evidence operations
Record
Supersede
Correct
Invalidate
The world changed.
valid time
a new period
transaction time
now
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
For example A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
If this produced an overpayment, the classification rule reads the operation as the world having changed.
Select an operation. Supersede and Correct both replace an earlier claim, but only Correct says the earlier claim was wrong about its own period. That is what separates a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
That distinction is the reason the model exists. It is a policy rule expressed in the shape of the data, and it can be applied consistently because the operation that produced a recalculation is recorded on the record itself rather than inferred afterwards.
The operation is an input to the classification rather than the whole of it. Who caused the error matters too, and a client who concealed a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. What the model guarantees is narrower and more useful: the question is answerable at all, from the record, rather than reconstructed by whoever is looking at the file today.
Where a conventional record gives up
Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
What the ministry believed about the household in each of those eight months.
When the ministry changed its mind, and on what evidence.
What start date the ministry now asserts.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date and an audit entry recording that a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot answer the first at all. The eight monthly payments are left looking like errors, when at the time each was the correct application of what was then known.
The operations, formally
Operation
Valid time
Transaction time
Meaning
RecordEvidence
asserted period
now
We learned a new fact
SupersedeEvidence
new period
now
The world changed
CorrectEvidence
same period
now
We were wrong about the world
InvalidateEvidence
closed
now
The assertion should never have existed
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The third date, and the history problem
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, and it exists because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
When old records are brought across, they all arrive on the same day. If that migration date becomes the "when we learned it" date for every inherited record, then every historical fact appears to have been learned simultaneously. Supersede and Correct become indistinguishable across the whole pre-cutover record, and the overpayment classification rule cannot run against the records where most overpayments actually sit.
The third axis holds the date the predecessor system asserted the fact, where that can be read out of the old record. It is frequently unknowable, so it carries a confidence marker, and where the answer is unknown the system says so rather than guessing.
valid time
The period in the world for which the fact holds.
Set by whoever asserts it, from the source.
transaction time
When this system learned it.
Set at recording. Never changes.
legacy assertion time
When the previous system asserted it, if that can be decoded.
Set at migration. Often unknown, and marked as such.
Three dates on every assertion. The third is nullable; the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than substituting the migration date.
This cannot be added later. Events are immutable: a field can be introduced with a default, but it cannot be filled in retroactively, because the source was either decoded at migration or it was not. The decision has to be made before the first production record is written.
Confidence values and replay behaviour
legacy_asserted_at is accompanied by legacy_assertion_confidence, which takes DECODED (read directly from the legacy record or audit trail), INFERRED (derived from a related artefact by a documented rule) or UNKNOWN.
On UNKNOWN, any consumer computing a knowledge-state answer (the overpayment classification rule, a tribunal reconstruction view, a disclosure history) must return INDETERMINATE. Projections that answer only valid-time questions ignore the field.
Retroactive recalculation runs off valid time, which a competent migration preserves, so recalculation is unaffected. What breaks without the third axis is narrower: the question of what the ministry knew and when, which is crucial for the integrity of our processes.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

A PWD* designation granted in July.
It takes effect from March.
Four months of payments were correct when they were made, and are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been entitled to. Our current system keeps only the second, rewriting history rather than recording it. What did we know, how can it be proven, and when? The future captures all of it, rather than ignoring it.

The month being asked about
Ask about May valid time

Asked in Jun about May, the system reports a monthly entitlement of $1,060.
Current version of the record: At application in March, no disability designation is in place.
Today the system reports $1,535.50 for May. The payment actually made that month was correct when it was issued, and is now an underpayment of $475.50.
Move either slider. The left one changes the month you are asking about. The right one changes the month you are asking in. The hard horizontal edge is the July decision reaching back over every month before it, which is what a retroactive determination looks like when both axes are kept.
Current State
Case management encompasses a vast array of services and processes across the Ministries of Children and Family Development and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. The gamut of assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss-recovery, and client support all require rich contextual information for workers to respond with awareness, compassion, integrity, and efficiency. This system is life critical - a wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
The systems doing the work are a pair, an Oracle Siebel Custom Relationship Management application adapted for use in government and a mainframe system dating back to 1982. They run in parallel, and together administer the core programming. All attempts to phase out the mainframe aborted or failed.
The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
Evidence, not 'facts'
The system will not store "this person is an adult." It stores, "on 14 July, AI Agent ID-33422 read the uploaded image of identification and determined the identity to match the case and the date of birth to be April 22, 1988. Business rules determine they're an adult." Who or what decided, when, and on what basis are part of the record rather than PDF forms attached to it or external to the system altogether.
Evidence
Apt boundaries
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very diverse portfolio. Yet our current system shoehorns this diversity into a fixed, rigid model. This is how designs drift and become brittle. Each of the program families gets its own model.
Domains
A decision you can re-run
Every entitlement decision stores the rules, the engine, the facts it saw, its own reasoning and outcomes. Four days later for a manager or years later at a tribunal, the decision can be replayed rather than reconstructed from memory.
Determinations
Why do backdates matter?
Social sector case management can be viewed as constructing a consistent timeline as information arrives. That information doesn't arrive consistently in order and past events can reframe current and futures ones. In the retroactive designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed. Someone on assistance has no reserve to absorb that. The same machinery runs in the other direction, and it lands on the same person who must pay back the overage.
When someone is paid more than they were entitled to, the money is treated one of two ways. If the client's circumstances changed and they reported it late, it is a recoverable overpayment, and the ministry takes it back at $10 a month out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry already held the information and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not be the one carrying it.
Telling those apart requires knowing when the ministry knew. That is a transaction-time question. A system that records only when a fact was true, or that stamps every migrated record with the date it was migrated, cannot answer it. The existing overpayment backlog sits almost entirely in records from before any cutover.
Mispayment is only one simple example. Nearly every claim a client makes must be corroborated by evidence. This cycle of claim, evidence and substantiation is the "core loop" of how social assistance is handled.
How this is modelled
Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions: valid_time (the period in the world for which the fact holds), recorded_at (when this system learned it), and legacy_asserted_at (when the predecessor system asserted it, where that can be decoded from the legacy record).
The third axis is nullable and carries a confidence enumeration of DECODED, INFERRED or UNKNOWN. On UNKNOWN, any consumer computing a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE rather than silently substituting the migration timestamp.
None of this can be added later. Events are immutable, so a field can be added with a default but cannot be populated retroactively. The axis has to exist before the first production event is written.
What this site covers
These pages set out the domain model and the reasoning behind the choices that are least conventional or intuitive. They contain both a plain language explanation and a rigorous technical articulation of how these concepts work in practice.
Current State is worth reading if you're unfamiliar with ICM/MIS. The proposed architecture's merits are clearest when compared to the conventional methods.

Appeals & Reconsideration
Apt boundaries
Archiving the software guarantees you can identify it. It does not guarantee that anything in twenty years can run it. The operating system, the processor architecture and the container runtime all have shorter lives than a child protection record, which is retained for ninety years.
Ask a typical case management system why a person received a particular amount in March 2022 and it will recalculate. It will use today's rules, today's data and today's software, and report the answer with confidence. That answer may be right. There is no way to tell, and no way to show a tribunal the difference.
Ask about
Asked in
Assembling the facts means reading across several stores that update independently. Two decisions issued seconds apart, where one store is briefly behind, can legitimately see different worlds. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far detects it. The design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events, so a later reader can tell which view of the world a decision was made against.

This system is life critical - a wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.

Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions:
Every evidence type needs a records determination before it can be used, which puts the records office on the critical path.
Every read is more complex. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and reporting has to specify which point in time it means.
Every recurring task a caseworker performs has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as it is actually delivered.
Every rule is labelled with what kind of decision it produces: an administrative decision that requires reasons, a decision that a person must make before it takes effect, or an intermediate calculation that affects nobody on its own.

Merge and split are built in from the first day rather than added later. The previous system's audit found duplicate records at scale, with search described as ineffective and exact-match only. Retrofitting merge into a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible, because by then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would be stable.

Provider & Outcome
Published events and the boundary test
Pure: no clock, no database, no service calls.
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine provides this on its own; it is enforced by the shell around the engine. The engine evaluates in-process against a snapshot passed by value, which is what makes byte-identical replay achievable rather than aspirational.
Rather than leave that unresolved, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.

Social sector case management can be viewed as constructing a consistent timeline as information arrives. That information doesn't arrive consistently in order and past events can reframe current and futures ones. In the retroactive designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed. Someone on assistance has no reserve to absorb that. The same machinery runs in the other direction, and it lands on the same person who must pay back the overage.
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. They are owned by platform teams and used by everyone. The distinction matters because a platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a seventeenth domain model without anyone chartering it.

Storing the answer is not enough, and storing the answer plus the rules is still not enough. Five artefacts are bound into the record at the moment the decision is made.
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently, and that is where the remaining gap sits.

System residency is a legal requirement

Template versions and content hashes have to be retained for as long as the decisions that reference them.
That constraint sounds academic. It is what makes the next part possible: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
That convention produced a section most architecture documents do not have: a list of things the authors believed at the outset and then disproved. Eleven assumptions were tested and failed. Two examples.
That distinction is the reason the model exists. It is a policy rule expressed in the shape of the data, and it can be applied consistently because the operation that produced a recalculation is recorded on the record itself rather than inferred afterwards.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. An adverse determination emits its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it because the classification says it must, not because somebody remembered.
The Future of Case Management IT
The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The architecture carries 40 open verification items and 30 items that must be resolved before the design is frozen. Three are worth naming here because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
The architecture document marks every claim with how well it is supported: verified against a primary source, internally confirmed but not publicly checkable, derived by arithmetic from marked inputs, or unverified. Unverified claims carry an owner and a date by which someone must resolve them.
The argument against a single model
The assertion is withdrawn. It remains visible in the history as withdrawn.
The assertion should never have existed
The case model for child care subsidy.

The case model for employment services.
The conventional move is a single configurable case model shared across programs.
The decision can be replayed.
The design is not a simple contradiction of the current system. It is the result of an interrogation as to why a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of intelligent, well-intended, capable people can fail to meet the needs of the organizations it is meant to serve. The conclusion is that the mismatch is not about what is present in the current system, but what is absent, ignored, or externalized.
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. It does not read the clock, does not query a database, and does not call another service while it runs. Everything it needs is handed to it.
The design still keeps systems in Canada, because cloud policy independently requires Canadian data centres. What changed is the stated reason, which is now policy rather than law.
The determination function, the decision record, the bound artefacts.
The determination reproduces perfectly and still fails to answer the question actually asked, which is often about the letter.
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
The earlier assertion was never right. The replacement covers exactly the same period.

The evidence succession set, verification policy, the four operations, three time axes.
The facts have to be assembled before the decision runs, and assembling them consistently is its own problem.
The facts it saw

The most consequential choice in this design is where to draw lines between parts of the system, and then to defend those lines. Twelve domain models, one of which is really five, so sixteen in total.
The one place money leaves the ministry.
The operation is an input to the classification rather than the whole of it. Who caused the error matters too, and a client who concealed a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. What the model guarantees is narrower and more useful: the question is answerable at all, from the record, rather than reconstructed by whoever is looking at the file today.

The reasoning
The record has to hold the world as it was, not a pointer to the world as it is.
The rule classifying a recalculation as recoverable or as administrative error reads the evidence operation that produced it.
The rules
The rules are maintained as a written specification, with a test suite that any re-implementation must reproduce. The suite is kept independent of the engine from the first day, so this transition costs nothing when it arrives.
The smallest rule surface, which is why it is captured first.
The software itself is archived and tested quarterly to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that actually re-execute.
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record, and re-running is no longer offered. This is what a paper file has always been.

The systems doing the work are a pair, an Oracle Siebel Custom Relationship Management application adapted for use in government and a mainframe system dating back to 1982. They run in parallel, and together administer the core programming. All attempts to phase out the mainframe aborted or failed.

The third date, and the history problem
The three stages are a real sequence, which is why they are numbered. The last is defensible because it was declared in advance rather than discovered during a hearing.
The two questions a tribunal asks are what was true and what the ministry knew. They need separate axes. The third axis exists only because fifteen years of records arrive from a system that is still running, and collapsing their history into the migration date would make an entire class of question unanswerable.
The version number survives but the executable does not. An identifier is worthless once the vendor stops serving that tag.
The world changed
The world changed.
There are exactly two ways to talk
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have limited computer access: a worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
These design pages set out how the proposal resolves these conditions. The clearest place to see the connection is
These pages set out the domain model and the reasoning behind the choices that are least conventional or intuitive. They contain both a plain language explanation and a rigorous technical articulation of how these concepts work in practice.
This cannot be added later. Events are immutable: a field can be introduced with a default, but it cannot be filled in retroactively, because the source was either decoded at migration or it was not. The decision has to be made before the first production record is written.
This is the part most likely to drift, because every new requirement produces a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model has been rebuilt in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
This is what a decision-maker reads out at a hearing.
This isn't simply an auditing nicety, it eliminates the cognitive drag; the mismatch between how the system handles data and how frontline staff operate. Significant effort is spent substantiating evidence against claims, this is done manually and is not a properly modeled first class activity despite it being, numerically, the most common task workers perform. Social workers must spend hours mapping their notes and activities to a different structure - serving the software, rather than their clients.
Three dates on every assertion. The third is nullable; the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than substituting the migration date.
Three systems
Three things have moved underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, possibly several times. The software itself was upgraded, and a rules engine upgrade can alter how the same rule evaluates without anyone noticing until someone appeals.

Treating a decision as a function
Two bodies of source material sit behind this. The technical design documents for the current release of the existing system, 57 of them, describing the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting. And the 326 service-delivery procedures describing how the work is done.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very diverse portfolio. Yet our current system shoehorns this diversity into a fixed, rigid model. This is how designs drift and become brittle. Each of the program families gets its own model.
Two of eleven assumptions that did not survive testing. Recording them makes the design reviewable; an architecture whose failed premises are invisible cannot be checked.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters are deliberately opposite. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive the systems that implement it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it is accountable for its own disbandment.
Two systems
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, and it exists because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Valid time

What 326 service-delivery procedures show about how the work is actually done.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Making them share a lifecycle means every change to one is negotiated with everyone else. The model becomes something nobody can change, and the programme starts removing scope to avoid changing it. The previous programme here merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope, for exactly this reason.

What this site covers
When old records are brought across, they all arrive on the same day. If that migration date becomes the "when we learned it" date for every inherited record, then every historical fact appears to have been learned simultaneously. Supersede and Correct become indistinguishable across the whole pre-cutover record, and the overpayment classification rule cannot run against the records where most overpayments actually sit.
When someone is paid more than they were entitled to, the money is treated one of two ways. If the client's circumstances changed and they reported it late, it is a recoverable overpayment, and the ministry takes it back at $10 a month out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry already held the information and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not be the one carrying it.

Whether a person owes money back depends on whether the ministry knew something and failed to act. A current value with a change log beside it cannot answer that reliably, because the log is not part of the decision path.

Which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes are all defined in an Excel workbook that 56 procedures refer to. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. Priority and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, maintained by hand.
